lesson.title: The Toolkit for Taming Indeterminate Forms
lesson.summary: Algebraic limit techniques are the family of methods, including factoring, combining fractions, and dividing by the highest power of x, used to rewrite an expression that produces an indeterminate form into an equivalent one that direct substitution can handle.
lesson.body:
Every specific method used so far for resolving an indeterminate form, canceling a shared factor for a 0 over 0 rational function, or dividing through by the highest power of x for an infinity over infinity rational function, is really one instance of a single unifying idea. That idea is the algebraic limit technique: when direct substitution produces an indeterminate form, rewrite the expression algebraically into a new expression that agrees with the original everywhere near the point in question, except possibly exactly at that point, and whose direct substitution actually works. The key fact making this legal is that a limit describes behavior near a point, never behavior at the point itself, so any algebraic manipulation that only changes the function's value at the single troublesome point, or is undefined there while remaining identical everywhere nearby, leaves the limit completely unaffected.

Several named strategies fall under this umbrella, each suited to a different kind of expression. Factoring and canceling a common factor works well for rational functions producing 0 over 0. Rationalizing, meaning multiplying by a conjugate expression, works well when square roots are involved and factoring alone cannot remove the radical. Combining separate fractions into a single fraction over a common denominator often exposes a cancelable factor that was hidden while the pieces were kept apart. Dividing every term by the highest power of the variable handles infinity over infinity situations for rational functions. Each of these is worth its own detailed practice, and two of them, factoring and rationalizing, are covered individually next.

Here is a worked example using the fraction combining strategy, since it has not been demonstrated yet. Find the limit as x approaches 0 of the quantity 1 over (x plus 2), minus 1 over 2, all divided by x. Substituting x equals 0 directly into the inner expression gives 1 over 2 minus 1 over 2, which is 0, and dividing that 0 by x, which is also 0 at x equals 0, gives the 0 over 0 form, confirming this is indeterminate and that factoring the numerator alone will not help, since the numerator is not a polynomial in an obviously factorable shape.

Combine the two fractions in the numerator over their common denominator, 2 times (x plus 2). This gives, in the numerator, 2 minus (x plus 2), all over 2(x plus 2), which simplifies to negative x over 2(x plus 2). The full expression is then this quantity divided by x, which equals negative x over (2(x plus 2) times x). For x not equal to 0, the x in the numerator cancels with the x from the outer division, leaving negative 1 over (2(x plus 2)). Now substitute x equals 0: negative 1 over (2 times 2), which is negative 1 over 4.

A numerical check confirms this. At x equal to 0.001, 1 over 2.001 is approximately 0.499750, minus 0.5 gives approximately negative 0.000250, and dividing that by 0.001 gives approximately negative 0.250, matching negative 1 over 4 closely. This example used the indeterminate form recognition from before and the same core cancellation principle used for the zero over zero case, just applied to a fraction that first needed to be combined into a single piece before any cancellation was visible.
